plan.angle: Climate foundation first, made visible at walking height. One shared, deterministic annual climate field, aware of obliquity and lapse rate, feeds the classifier, the orbit and tile colour, forest presence, tree species and the ground shader. A pure season module is prepared in parallel for the next 4D increment.
plan.thesis:
The repo has no climate model. Three unsynchronised copies of an ad-hoc rule decide what the ground looks like:
- terrain.ts:222-245 sets colour from pre-landform height, with a +0.17 dry belt.
- surface-biomes.ts:14-31 is the classifier. It uses post-landform height and has no belt.
- planet-renderer.ts:830 holds a body-level turf gate.

The snow rule adds latitude and altitude terms, which puts the equatorial snowline near 20.8 km. That is why the 18 km equatorial summit on Maithea renders as brown soil with grazers. The rule also ignores obliquity, which is drawn uniformly over 0-180 degrees, so it is physically inverted on about 36-40% of worlds. Forests sit in an absolute 160-2300 m band. Species are hashed without reference to their niches. The close-range PBR overwrites every climate tint with 68% brown dirt.

The increment:
- Wave 0 (now, new files only): src/surface-climate.ts (annual mean temperature from a det-math insolation table, lapse rate, seasonal half-range, the shared dry belt, snow fraction, treeline, forest suitability, climate code), src/habitat-suitability.ts (niche evaluator, family affinity, weighted rendezvous helper, fauna habitat types) and src/season.ts + src/sun-frame.ts (closed-form seasons in the exact rendered-sun convention, no consumers yet).
- Wave 1, after the fauna merge and the owner's calibration answer: three disjoint packages wire the climate into the classifier, the orbit/tile colour and the ground shader.
- Wave 2: forest presence and species binding.
- Wave 3: integration, captures, perf.

Presence and kind decisions read only annual statistics. Seasons stay presentation-only and arrive in the next increment. Every output change comes with its own version bump. Digest gates stay differential, and REFERENCE is never moved.

(3) `climateForcingFor(body, opts?:{anchorTempK?:number})` returns a frozen ClimateForcing:
- `{anchorTempK: opts?.anchorTempK ?? body.temperatureK, obliquityRad: min(t, PI-t) with t=spinStateFor(body).axialTiltRad, water: body.water, frozen: body.type==='Ice world', habitat: temperateHabitat(body), moistureSeed: Number(hash64(body.seed+'/macro-v1')&0xffffffffn), qMean: Float64Array(65), qAmp: Float64Array(65), provenance: {anchorTempK:'catalogue', obliquityRad:'catalogue', table:'derived-heuristic'}}`.
- Cache it in a module Map keyed `body.seed+'|'+anchorTempK`, capped at 64 entries with FIFO eviction. Eviction must not change values; test cold vs warm.
- Table: for k=0..64 set x=k/64 (sin latitude), cosPhi=sqrt(1-x*x). For j=0..255 set lambda=(j+.5)*2*PI/256, sinDelta=sine(eps)*sine(lambda), cosDelta=sqrt(1-sinDelta^2) (written as multiplication).
- Daily-mean insolation: if cosPhi<1e-12 then Q=max(0,sinDelta); else c=clamp(-(x*sinDelta)/(cosPhi*cosDelta),-1,1), h0=detAcos(c), Q=(h0*x*sinDelta+cosPhi*cosDelta*sqrt(1-c*c))/PI.
- qMean[k] = the mean of Q over j, and qAmp[k] = (max-min)/2. Normalise both by the area mean of qMean, which is a trapezoid over x because dA is proportional to d(sin lat). Eccentricity is ignored (a uniform factor in the annual mean); document this.
- Only det-math, + - * /, sqrt, min, max, floor and abs are allowed.
(4) `surfaceClimate(forcing)` returns `(d:V3, heightM:number, out:ClimateSample)=>out`. No allocation and no hash64 per call. With x=|d[1]|, interpolate the tables linearly at x*64 to get q and qa, then:

- `seasonalHalfRangeK = SEASON_K*qa*(1-MARITIME*water)`
- `warmestMonthK = annualMean + seasonalHalfRange`
- `legacyMoisture = noise(d[0]*5+13, d[1]*5+37, d[2]*5+19, moistureSeed+30)`, the exact classifier expression

- `effectiveMoisture = legacyMoisture - BELT_MOISTURE*dryBelt01`

- `snowFraction = frozen ? 1 : water>0 ? clamp01((T_SNOW_K-annualMean)/SNOW_RAMP_K) : 0`
- `treeline01 = clamp01((warmestMonthK-T_TREE_WARMEST_K)/TREE_RAMP_K)`

(1) src/sun-frame.ts is pure, with no three import.
- `spinCompensated(rawSun:V3, tiltRad, spinAngleRad):V3` reproduces THREE Vector3.applyAxisAngle about X by -tilt and then about Y by -angle. Continuous presentation values, so Math.cos and Math.sin are allowed.
- `subsolarSinLat(rawSun, tiltRad) = s_y*cos(tilt) + s_z*sin(tilt)`, which is the y component after the X rotation. Spin about Y does not change y.

(2) src/season.ts, with `SEASON_VERSION='atlas-season-1'`.
- `seasonBasis(body, sys)` takes no t and is cached per body.seed.
  - Year: yearNs is the phaseAt period of the orbit that carries the body around the star. That is the body's own orbit for a planet and the parent planet's orbit for a moon, computed as BigInt(Math.round(2π/ω·1e9)), the same as phaseAt.
  - Sample k=0..63 dates t_k = k*yearNs/64n, offset by any fixed epoch (the basis is periodic). At each date compute rawSun from the same bodyPosition(sys.stars[0]) − bodyPosition(body) pair main.ts uses, then subsolar latitude δ_k via subsolarSinLat, then the distance factor (a/r)^2.
  - For 19 latitude bands (−90..90 in 10-degree steps), compute daily-mean insolation Q(φ,δ,r), and from it the annual mean Q̄(φ) and the complex Fourier harmonics F1(φ) and F2(φ) over k.
- `seasonAt(basis, t:bigint, windowNs=0n)`: phase = ((t mod yearNs)+yearNs) mod yearNs, as a BigInt Euclidean modulo; then φ01 = Number(phase)/Number(yearNs).
  - subsolarSinLat is computed exactly at t from the bodyPosition pair, not interpolated.
  - `tempAnomalyK[19]` is the closed-form periodic solution of C·dT/dt = F − B·T per harmonic: T_k = κ·(anchorT/4)·(F_k/Q̄_global)/(1 + i·k·ω·τ), with κ=0.6 and τ = 20 d + 100 d·body.water (heuristic-v1). Each harmonic is multiplied by sinc(k·ω·W/2) for window W, so W=0 is exact and a long window decays to the annual mean.
  - It returns `{yearNs, phase01, subsolarSinLat, distanceFactor, tempAnomalyK, slowRotator: spinPeriodS/yearS>0.1}`.
- Also export `FaunaSeasonContext` and `faunaSeasonContext(basis,t)`, which returns {version, yearNs, seasonPhase01(latRad), tempAnomalyK(latRad), daylightFraction(latRad)}. These are for presentation only and must never feed presence.
- Nothing in src imports these modules in this increment.

It fixes the verified root causes at their source: the additive-latitude snow rule (equatorial snowline about 20.8 km, from surface-biomes.ts:22 and terrain.ts:222-225), the pre- vs post-landform colour height (terrain.ts:426 `color: sample.color`), the missing dry belt in the classifier, the absolute 160-2300 m forest band, and hash-only species binding (tree-species-recipe.ts:28, NOT :57 as the proposal says). It uses no new textures and no new tile attributes. Weaknesses: the rain-shadow probe is an unvalidated heuristic. W1-F adds an unused climateForcingAt API and a main.ts:665 surveyKey edit; neither is needed, because surveyKey already includes TERRAIN_VERSION. It also implies BIOSPHERE profile-constant edits that are not needed.

scores.angle: VISIBLE-GROUND-FIRST (climate covers, per-vertex groundCover attribute, Biome-Lab understory, rock coats)
scores.notes: Highest walking-height payoff, but too much for one round. It needs 9 packages. W0b plumbing touches planet-renderer.ts, planet-tiles.ts, planet-worker.ts and renderer-memory.ts, all after the fauna merge, and it serialises the round. The new Uint8x4 attribute adds +9,768 B per tile while shore settle is already at 0.934 of the 0.94 ceiling. Understory work moves life-cpu-digest (flora-field and planet-renderer are LIFE_FILES), and rock coats add yet another surface. Its good ideas are adopted in a cheaper form: ratio-detail PBR, taking sand off the dirt photo, and the snow-reads-as-dunes fix, all without the new attribute. Understory assemblages and covers become the next increment.

scores.angle: TIME-AND-LIFE-FIRST (closed-form seasons as uniforms, phenology, dated forest-belt shift, owner-gated brightening)
scores.notes: Best for the 4D goal, and seasons as uniforms only is very safe for determinism. It leaves the biome problems the user asked about unfixed at the simulation level, though. The classifier keeps its legacy snow and forest rules, so herds and leafy shrubs stay on what is visually snow, and the orbit view and the ground still disagree. Package C (dated bucket) is inert until the owner-gated stellar brightening (E) lands. The pure season.ts and sun-frame.ts modules, which are new files with no consumers, are adopted as a parallel Wave-0 package so the next increment can wire seasons onto a corrected climate.

openQuestionsForUser: How white should Maithea get? Maithea's land is very high (median about 6.5 km), so the new temperature-with-altitude model makes much of it snow. Share of land with heavy snow (proposal-probe figures, which Wave 0 will re-measure): today about 35%; a gentler 4.0 K/km cooling rate gives about 58% (my default); the physically correct 6.5 K/km gives about 79%. Which do you want?

Tilt: each planet's axial tilt is drawn anywhere from 0 to 180 degrees, so about 36-40% of worlds are tilted past 54 degrees and should have warm poles and an icy equator. Honour that (my default; it matches the sun you already see in the sky), or redraw tilts to be Earth-like? Redrawing changes the visible sun, day/night and rings on many worlds and needs a catalogue/spin version bump.
Every existing bookmark will show a one-time 'this predates the current model' notice, because the terrain version and the model manifest change. Is that acceptable?

Should planet temperature account for how bright the star is, and should stars slowly brighten over billions of years? Both are physically correct, but about 83% of currently forest-eligible water worlds would leave the habitable band. I've left this for a later increment unless you want it sooner.

Seasons come in the next increment and affect looks only (snow line, grass browning, autumn leaves, bare winter trees). Above roughly a year every few seconds of playback they would average out instead of flickering. Is that the behaviour you want? And is it OK if, until the classifier itself becomes seasonal, animals can stand on winter-only snow?
A wetland biome needs inland water, which stays withdrawn as you asked. Do you want it back at some point, or should wetland stay lab-only?

observations: SETUP (verified): The planet is LETHRA-001 / G001/C2128,0,1/0/planet/1 ('Maithea'), an Oceanic world with radius 5195 km, catalog temperatureK 284 and water 0.415. I took the GPU lock only through tests/helpers/gpu-lock.mjs, in 5 holds of 14 s, 176 s, 140 s, 27 s and 42 s. The lock was released each time and the directory is gone. git status is clean.

HARNESS NOTE (verified): Headless Chrome with --use-angle=d3d11 rendered on the AMD Radeon iGPU (0x13C0), not the RTX. Frame p95 was 300-1200 ms. With ?walk=, equatorLowland, midLatForest and midLatSnowMountain never reached grounded within 40-70 s. They stayed at 'LANDING · refining nearby ground', hovering about 12 m above the ground. dryUpland, highMountain, polar and coast did reach grounded in 37-44 s. Without a ?heading= the hover camera kept a 90-degree-rolled orientation (first attempt). The fix was passing a level heading quaternion. Body axes equal world axes because the terrain mesh is never rotated.

LABEL COVERAGE (verified by sampling 150k Fibonacci points on walkable land, using biomeClassifier with groundHeightM): Alpine/polar snow 28,873; Mountain meadow 26,329; Dry upland 17,104; Temperate ground 4,892; Rock escarpment 4,774; Coastal sand 533. So more than 70% of dry land on this 'life-bearing' world is labelled snow or meadow above 2300 m. Most land sits very high. terrain.ts:207-208 clamps elevation to plus or minus 18,000 m times min(1, R/2e6), and Maithea has 18 km equatorial peaks.

SNOWLINE BUG (verified in code and on screen): surface-biomes.ts:21 has snow = clamp((lat-0.79)*7 + max(0,h-2600)/3300), and terrain.ts:222-225 uses the same formula. The latitude term is additive and strongly negative at low latitudes. That puts the snowline at about 20 km at the equator, about 4.5 km at 45 degrees, and 2.6 km only at about 52 degrees. Shot 04-ground-highMountain.png is at 18,066 m and latitude 1.7 degrees. The classifier labels it 'Dry upland' with weights soil 1, snow 0. It renders as warm brown soil with leafy forbs and herds of grazers, the same as the lowland. Ecologically this is impossible: no alpine zone, no treeline-to-tundra transition, no thin-air sky.

EQUATOR LOWLAND (04-ground-equatorLowland*.png; 303 m, latitude 10 degrees, Temperate ground, forestPotential=true, about 700 trees visible): This is an open stand of narrow spruce/fir-like conifers with a few broadleaf trees on uniform bare olive-brown soil. It has scattered forb seedlings, no grass sward, no litter, no shrub layer, and no canopy closure. To an ecologist it reads as a boreal or montane conifer plantation, not a tropical or subtropical lowland. Latitude has no effect: the tree species binding ignores climate, consistent with the bindTreeSpecies lead.

MID-LATITUDE FOREST (04-ground-midLatForest*.png; 1556 m, latitude 35.6 degrees, forestPotential=true): This is visually the same conifer stand on the same brown soil as the equator site. The only difference is heavier fog or aerial perspective. There is no distinct structure or composition, so the equator and mid-latitude forests cannot be told apart. Grazers walk among the trees.

DRY UPLAND (04-ground-dryUpland*.png; 259 m, latitude 23.6 degrees, moisture 0.417, just under the 0.43 'Dry upland' cut): The same brown soil and forb seedlings, with no trees, scattered small rocks, and large herds on the skyline. It is distinct from the forest only because trees are missing. Ground colour, plant life-forms, rock exposure and sparseness all match the 'lowland' look, and there is no xeric shrub, bunchgrass or pale caliche/sand tint. Biome Lab's dry-scrub preset (tan ground, sage bushes, angular rocks) does much better than the planet here.

COAST (04-ground-coast*.png; 93 m, latitude 14.6 degrees, Coastal sand, weights sand 0.42 / soil 0.58): This looks the same as the dry upland: brown soil, forbs, herds. No beach sand tint, dune grass or strand vegetation is visible within about 100 m. The ocean is not visible from either heading. The 0.42 sand weight produces no visible colour shift.

SNOW MOUNTAIN (04-ground-midLatSnowMountain*.png; 3975 m, latitude 53.9 degrees, label 'Mountain meadow', weights soil 0.46 / snow 0.54): The camera hovered about 12 m up because the landing never completed. The ground blends to a muddy sage-olive grey, not white snow over tundra. Strong concentric ripple or ring banding covers the ground texture, which looks like a sand-ripple detail normal tiling across km-scale slopes. A few animals are present. It is not legible as alpine meadow or snowfield. Label and weights disagree visually: 'meadow' should look green and herbaceous, and 54% snow should look patchy white.

POLAR (04-ground-polar*.png; 688 m, latitude 68 degrees, snow 0.96): Bright white ground with regular aeolian-style ripples reads as white sand dunes, not snow or ice. The ripple detail looks shared with sand. There are scattered leafy shrubs and rocks, plus distant animals, on 96% snow cover. That vegetation is ecologically wrong: it should be bare snow or polar desert with lichen or cushion plants at most. There are no sastrugi, ice blue or tundra transition. This is still the most visually distinct site of the six.

ORBIT (03-orbit.png is the default camera, almost all night side; 03-orbit-rot4.png is the sunlit limb): The land reads tan, ochre and grey-brown with white patches (clouds and/or snow) and ocean. There is almost no green anywhere, although the ground has dense conifer stands at 10 and 35 degrees latitude. Verified cause: terrain.ts:234-241 mixes the land colour toward grey-brown [134,124,107] by (elev-1500)/4300, and most land is high. It also adds an arid push for latitudes 0.18 to 0.52 (sin-latitude), and only moisture-driven green [40,89,48]. Forest presence never feeds the orbit colour, so a forested world looks like a desert from orbit. The default orbit camera on load also faces the night side, a separate presentation issue.

BIOME LAB (01-biome-lab-overview.png and 02-biome-lab-{conifer,dry-scrub,alpine}-ground.png): The 128 m flat test plots are clearly distinct from one another. Woodland has round broadleaf crowns on mid-green ground. Conifer has tall dark cone trees, slabs, a grass understory and canopy footprint 13.4%. Dry scrub has tan ground, sage bushes, bunch grass and angular rock, with canopy 0%. Alpine has pale sage ground, slabs, cushion shrubs and 0% canopy. Each has its own recipe list and planned-fauna pairing ('Cone eater', 'Drought browser', and so on). The look is low-poly flat-shaded under a black sky, and fauna are listed as 'planned' and not rendered. None of this per-biome composition or ground tint reaches the planet surface, which is consistent with the lead that biome-ecology.ts is used only by biome-lab.ts.

CROSS-SITE SUMMARY (inferred from the screenshots): On the planet, only 3 visual 'biomes' can be told apart: (a) conifer stand on brown soil, (b) brown soil with forbs and herds (dry upland, coast and the 18 km summit all look the same), and (c) white rippled ground (polar). The 54%-snow mountain is a muddy in-between. The ground albedo is one olive-brown soil everywhere except snow. Understory is the same forb or seedling mix at every site, and grazer herds are present at every site from 93 m to 18 km and on 96% snow. The time-of-capture date is the catalogue 'now', about 13.8 Gyr.
worstProblems: The snowline formula (surface-biomes.ts:21 and terrain.ts:222-225) makes the latitude term additive and strongly negative. The equatorial snowline lands near 20 km, and snow does not reach 2.6 km until about 52 degrees latitude. An 18 km equatorial summit (04-ground-highMountain.png) renders as warm brown soil with forbs and grazing herds, labelled 'Dry upland'. There is no altitudinal zonation: no treeline, alpine tundra, rock/scree or nival zone below about 50 degrees latitude.

The planet surface shows almost no biome differentiation. Equator lowland (10 degrees, 303 m) and mid-latitude forest (36 degrees, 1556 m) are the same open conifer stand on the same bare olive-brown soil. Dry upland, coastal sand (sand weight 0.42) and the 18 km summit all look the same: brown soil, forbs, herds. Ground albedo, understory life-forms and vegetation structure do not respond to climate, and a tropical lowland looks boreal.

Biome Lab composes 9 visibly distinct habitats with their own recipes, ground tints and fauna pairings, but none of it reaches the planet (biome-ecology.ts is used only by biome-lab.ts). The working biome vocabulary already exists and is simply not wired in.

Snow and polar ground read as sand. 96% snow at 68 degrees renders as white aeolian dune ripples with leafy shrubs on it. 54% snow at 4 km renders as muddy sage with strong concentric ripple banding, apparently a sand-ripple detail normal tiled at km scale. The leafy vegetation and grazers on near-total snow cover come from understory and fauna gating that ignores snow and temperature.

The orbit and ground views disagree. From orbit the forested world looks tan/ochre desert (terrain.ts:234-241 greys land above 1500 m and adds a 0.18-0.52 arid belt, and forest presence never feeds the orbit colour). On the ground there are dense conifer stands at 10 and 35 degrees. Separately, the default orbit camera loads facing the night side (03-orbit.png).

Testing and harness hazards for the implementation round: ?walk= landings stall at 'refining nearby ground' on the iGPU that headless d3d11 actually selects. Three of 7 sites never grounded within 40-70 s, and p95 frame time was 0.3-1.2 s. Without ?heading= the hover camera is rolled 90 degrees. Port 5220 is permanently occupied by an unrelated pi-host-web server. Any biome visual-regression script should pass an explicit heading, accept a hover-state capture, and choose a free port.
